title: Optimisation
body:
Optimisation is one of the most fundamental areas of numerical computing. From simple root finding to advanced machine learning, optimisation is everywhere. In this chapter, we will give you a brief overview of this topic and how the OCaml numerical library, Owl, supports basic optimisation methods.

Running the examples

Source: code/chap09_optimisation
Run: python3 scripts/run_chapter09.py

In utop, load this setup. The complete input is in sessions/chapter09.ml:

OCAML
open Owl_plplot;;
Owl_stats_prng.init 79;;

9.1 Objective Functions

Mathematical optimisation is the problem of finding the minima (or maxima) of a function, either as a closed-form solution if one exists, or numerically. [1] Formally, an optimisation problem can be expressed in the form:

minimise f0(𝐱), subject to fi(𝐱) ≤ bi,i = 1,2,…,m. (9.1)

The function f0 : 𝐑n →𝐑 is the optimisation target, called the objective function or cost function. 𝐱 is a vector of the optimisation variables, i.e. 𝐱 = [x1,x2,...xn]. An optimisation problem restricts the feasible values of the variables by zero or more constraints expressed as constraint functions fi : 𝐑n →𝐑 bounded by the bi. The goal is to find the optimal values of 𝐱 = 𝐱∗ that satisfy all constraints and attain the minimum of f0, if such values exist. The number of constraints m need not equal the number of variables n.

Solving an optimisation problem embodies the idea “maximise benefit/minimise cost with given constraints”, which applies to many real world problems including task scheduling, resource management, investment portfolio optimisation, logistics, aeronautical engineering, and competitive games [2]. Optimisation problems can be categorised into different types. The simplest are called linear optimisation (or linear programming) where the objective and constraint functions are affine (linear plus a constant). A linear function satisfies Eq. 9.2; constants can be separated from the linear parts in an LP formulation.

fi(𝛼𝑥 + 𝛽𝑦) = αfi(x) + βfi(y), (9.2)

Linear optimisation is important because non-negativity is a common constraint on real world quantities such as resource planning, and people are often interested in additive bounds. Additionally, many problems can be approximated by a linear model, e.g., production planning and transportation of divisible goods [3]. Many linear programmes can be solved efficiently with off-the-shelf tools, although problem size, sparsity and numerical conditioning matter. Discrete routing choices require additional integer constraints, and portfolio models that include a quadratic risk term are typically quadratic programmes.

Linear optimisation can be extended in various ways. For example, solving for a quadratic objective function under affine constraints is called quadratic programming; it is convex when the quadratic Hessian is positive semidefinite. Convexity requires

f(𝜃𝑥 + (1 − 𝜃)y) ≤ 𝜃𝑓(x) + (1 − 𝜃)f(y),0 ≤ 𝜃 ≤ 1,

for x,y in a convex domain. A convex optimisation problem has a convex objective and convex inequality constraint functions; any equality constraints must be affine. Convexity is an important dividing line: every local minimum of a convex problem is global, and many important convex problem classes admit efficient algorithms. It is not a blanket guarantee that every convex problem is easy or every non-convex problem is difficult. The textbook by Boyd and Vandenberghe [4] focuses on convex optimisation.

Alternatively, if we remove all the constraints from Eq. 9.1, it becomes an unconstrained optimisation problem. For a differentiable convex function on 𝐑n, a point x∗ is a global minimiser if and only if ∇ ⁡f(x∗) = 0; in one dimension this becomes f′(x∗) = 0. Such a point need not exist. In equality constrained optimisation, the constraints are equalities. For consistent affine equalities 𝐴𝑥 = b, we can parameterise the feasible set and eliminate the equalities, giving an unconstrained problem in fewer variables. General nonlinear equalities need not admit such a reduction.

Optimisation covers a very wide range of topics and techniques, and this chapter gives only a very brief introduction. The rest of this chapter focuses mainly on the unconstrained and local optimisation. We refer readers to Boyd and Vandenberghe [4] and Fletcher [5] for a more in-depth discussion. 1

9.2 Root Finding

Root finding is the process of finding variable values which make a function equal to zero. These variable values are the roots of the function. We have already seen examples of root finding in Chapter 2. Actually, it is not an optimisation problem, but the two topics are closely related, and understanding the techniques used in root finding is also helpful for us to understand some of the optimisation methods.

The bisection method is a simple iterative method to find roots. Let’s use f(x) = x2 − 2 as an example. The positive root of f(x) = 0 is x = 2 = 1.4142135623…. To find this solution, the bisection method proceeds as follows. We know the solution must be between 1 and 2, so first we set x to the mid-point x = 1.5. As x2 = 2.25 is larger than 2, x is too large so we try x = 11 4 next, which turns out to be too small. We then try 13 8, and so on, until a number is found, the square of which is close enough to 2. The bisection method is often slow to converge, halving the bracket width at each iteration. From an initial width of 1, 47 halvings reduce it below 10−14 in exact arithmetic. However, bisection is a solid and reliable method to find roots as long as the function is continuous on the bracket and its endpoint values have opposite signs. Owl provides the Owl_maths_root.bisec function that implements this method. The current Owl implementation requires a strict sign change; an endpoint that is already a root should be handled before calling it.

The Newton method (also known as the Newton-Raphson method) is more complex, using the derivative of the function f whose root is sought. It can converge faster near a simple root. It starts with an initial value x0, and iteratively updates the variable as follows until the change in consecutive values is deemed too small:

xn+1 = xn − f(xn) f′(xn). (9.3)

We can use the Algorithmic Differentiation module in Owl to perform the derivative calculation. Again, let’s find the root of x2 − 2 = 0 with this method using the following code, a direct translation of Eq. 9.3.

OCAML
open Algodiff.D

let f x = Maths.(x ** (F 2.) - (F 2.))

let _ =
  let x = ref 1. in
  for _ = 0 to 6 do
    let g = diff f (F !x) |> unpack_elt in
    let v = f (F !x) |> unpack_elt in
    x := !x -. v /. g;
    Printf.printf "%.15f\n" !x
  done;;

The code performs seven updates. By the fifth update the displayed 15 decimal places have stabilised:

OCAML SESSION
1.500000000000000
1.416666666666667
1.414215686274510
1.414213562374690
1.414213562373095
1.414213562373095
1.414213562373095

Near a simple root of a sufficiently smooth function, Newton’s method has quadratic convergence: the next error is of order the square of the current error. This requires a sufficiently close starting point and a nonzero derivative; convergence from an arbitrary initial point is not guaranteed. As a result, it is the basis of many powerful numerical methods, such as optimisation, multiplicative inverses of numbers and power series, and solving transcendental equations.

However, the Newton method requires a function to be differentiable. If computing the derivative is inconvenient, we can approximate it with a secant through two points – the Secant Method:

f′(x n) ≈ f(xn) − f(xn−1) xn − xn−1 . (9.4)

This method does not need explicit derivatives. Near a simple root, under suitable smoothness and starting-point assumptions, its convergence order is (1 + 5)∕2 ≈ 1.618, rather than Newton’s quadratic order. A zero difference in function values makes the secant step undefined. With the Secant method, two points are used at each iteration in approximating the derivative. An improved version, the Inverse Quadratic Interpolation (IQI) method, fits a quadratic to x as a function of f(x) at three points with distinct function values, then evaluates it at zero. This has the benefit that it’s fast at the later phase of the process at the cost of intermediate results being potentially very unstable.

These methods can be combined to make the even more powerful Brent’s method, a widely used method for a continuous function on a sign-changing bracket. It combines the robustness of the Bisection method with the fast iteration speed of Secant and IQI methods. The core idea is to use the fast algorithm whenever possible, but switch to the robust one when an interpolation step fails its acceptance safeguards. Owl_maths_root.brent implements Brent’s method. The above example can then be simply solved with a one-liner.

OCAML SESSION
# let f x = x *. x -. 2.;;
val f : float -> float = <fun>
# Owl_maths_root.brent f 0. 2.;;
- : float = 1.41421331999550248

9.3 Univariate Function Optimisation

Having briefly introduced several classic root-finding methods, we now turn to the main topic of this chapter: unconstrained optimisation problems. Let’s consider first a simple case where there is only one variable in the objective function. We will see in the next section that the same optimisation methods used for multivariate functions can be applied to the univariate case, but a method specialised for one dimension may be more economical. Understanding the optimisation of univariate functions is also an indispensable step towards understanding optimisation of multivariate ones.

9.3.1 Use Derivatives

For a differentiable function, an interior local extremum must be a stationary point, where the first derivative equals zero:

f′(x) = 0

This condition alone does not distinguish a minimum, a maximum or a stationary inflection point. It takes us back to our root finding solutions. If we already know the analytical form of f′(x), life becomes very easy. For example, if f(x) = x2 − x, then you can directly calculate the stationary point with f′(x) = 2x − 1. Otherwise, you can use the differentiation functions in Owl. Let’s look at an example of optimising an objective function with a hump shape:

f(x) = 1 (x − 0.3)2 + 0.01 + 1 (x − 0.9)2 + 0.04 − 6
OCAML
open Algodiff.D

let f x = Maths.(
  (F 1.) / ((x - F 0.3) ** (F 2.) + F 0.01) +
  (F 1.) / ((x - F 0.9) ** (F 2.) + F 0.04) - F 6.)

let g = diff f
let f' x = f (F x) |> unpack_flt
let g' x = g (F x) |> unpack_flt;;

To better understand the optimisation process, we can visualise the function and its derivative in Fig. 9.1.

You can then obtain candidate extremum locations by calling the Owl root finding functions, including Brent’s:

OCAML SESSION
# Owl_maths_root.brent g' 0. 0.4;;
- : float = 0.30037562625819042
# Owl_maths_root.brent g' 0.4 0.7;;
- : float = 0.63700940626897
# Owl_maths_root.brent g' 0.7 1.0;;
- : float = 0.892716303287079405

Brent’s method finds three stationary points in the specified brackets. Root finding alone does not classify them, but their second derivatives do: the points near 0.300376 and 0.892716 have negative curvature and are local maxima, while the point near 0.637009 has positive curvature and is a local minimum.

9.3.2 Golden Section Search

We are again confronted by the question: what if calculating the derivatives of a function is difficult, or analytical solutions are not available? That leads us to some search-based approaches. In the previous section, we saw how we can quickly reach the solution by continuously shrinking an interval that contains a root. The Golden Section Search is built on the same idea, and does not require calculating derivatives. Its interval-reduction guarantee assumes a continuous unimodal function on the search interval: decreasing towards a minimum and increasing afterwards [6].

As in the bisection method, Golden Section Search keeps shrinking intervals until they are “small enough”. The bisection method uses a tuple [a, b], and iteratively inserts a third point c to improve this tuple. This form of golden section search uses three numbers rather than two: [a, b, c], and seeks to iteratively improve this tuple by inserting a fourth number. Here a < b < c brackets a minimum, with f(b) < f(a) and f(b) < f(c). It contains two ranges: [a, b] and [b, c]. For every iteration, we need to find a new number d within one of the two ranges. For example, if we choose the d within [b, c], and if f(b) > f(d), then the new triplet becomes [b, d, c], otherwise the new triplet is chosen as [a, b, d]. With this approach, the range of this triplet keeps reducing until it is small enough and the minimum value can thus be found.

We also need to choose a suitable d point at each step. This approach first chooses the larger of the two ranges, either [a, b] or [b, c]. And then, instead of choosing the middle point in that range, it takes a fraction (3 −5)∕2 ≈ 0.381966 of the larger subinterval, measured from the central point towards the outer endpoint. Indeed, the name of this method comes from the Golden Ratio used in this step.

In general, this method is rather robust. With the initial interior point at a golden-section position and the unimodality assumption, each new interval has (5 − 1)∕2 ≈ 0.618034 times the previous width [6].

9.4 Multivariate Function Optimisation

The methods for univariate scenarios can be extended to multivariate optimisation problems. The equivalent of derivative in this multi-dimensional space is the gradient, already seen in Chap. 8. To find the extreme values of a function with multiple independent variables, we will introduce methods with and without using gradients.

9.4.1 Nelder-Mead Simplex Method

Derivative-free methods use function values without requiring gradients. One such method is the Nelder-Mead Simplex Method [7]. Its name refers to the geometric simplex, not to the algorithm being the simplest. It is often useful for small problems, but does not have a general convergence guarantee for arbitrary objectives.

The method utilises the concept of a simplex, namely the convex hull of n + 1 affinely independent vertices in an n-dimensional space, such as a triangle on a 2D plane. The basic idea of this method is to move a simplex gradually towards the lowest point on the function. In an N-dimensional space (where the function contains N variables), this simplex consists of N + 1 points. For example, for a function that has 2 variables, the simplex is a triangle; for 3 variables, a tetrahedron is used, etc.

Starting from an initial simplex, the method compares the function values at its vertices. At each step, it identifies the worst vertex p and reflects it through the centroid of the other vertices:

  1. if reflection improves on the best vertex, try an expansion further along that direction and retain the better of the reflected and expanded points;
  2. otherwise, if the reflected value is better than the second-worst value, accept the reflection;
  3. if not, try an outside or inside contraction, depending on whether reflection improved on the worst value;
  4. if contraction fails its improvement test, shrink the other vertices towards the best one.

Repeat until a stopping condition is met. Fig. 9.2 illustrates reflection, contraction and shrinking in two dimensions; expansion is not shown.

There are some other methods which do not rely on computing gradients, such as Powell’s method [11]. It performs one-dimensional minimisations along a set of directions and updates those directions. It can be a useful alternative to Nelder-Mead, but their relative speed and reliability depend on the problem.

9.4.2 Gradient Descent Methods

A descent method is an iterative optimisation process. [8] The idea is to start from an initial value, and then find a certain search direction along a function to decrease the value by certain step size until a stopping condition is met; convergence to a local minimum requires further assumptions. This process can be illustrated in Fig. 9.3.

We can thus describe the n-th iteration of descent method as:

  1. calculate a descent direction d;
  2. choose a step size α;
  3. update the location: xn+1 = xn + 𝛼 𝑑.

Repeat this process until a stopping condition is met, such as the update being smaller than a threshold.

Among descent methods, Gradient Descent is one of the most widely used algorithms to perform optimisation and forms the basis of many methods used to train neural networks. [9, 10] Based on the descent process above, Gradient Descent method uses the function gradient to decide its direction d, and can be described as:

  1. calculate a descent direction −∇ ⁡ 𝑓(xn);
  2. choose a step size α;
  3. update the location: xn+1 = xn − 𝛼 ∇ ⁡ 𝑓(xn).

Here ∇ ⁡ denotes the gradient. The step-size parameter α is also called learning rate. In a gradient descent process, when searching for the minimum, the point always follows the direction that is the direction represented by the negative gradient. The actual update length is α∥∇ ⁡f(xn)∥, and a step that is too large need not decrease the objective.

Again, it is straightforward to implement this process with the algorithmic differentiation module in Owl. Let’s look at one example. Here we use the Rosenbrock function [12] which is usually used as a performance test for optimisation problems. The function is defined as:

f(x,y) = (a − x)2 + b(y − x2)2. (9.5)

The parameters are usually set as a = 1 and b = 100.

OCAML
open Algodiff.D
module N = Dense.Ndarray.D

let rosenbrock a =
  let x = Mat.get a 0 0 in
  let y = Mat.get a 0 1 in
  Maths.( (F 100.) * (y - (x ** (F 2.))) ** (F 2.) +
    (F 1. - x) ** (F 2.) |> sum');;

Let’s apply the gradient descent method and observe the optimisation trajectory:

OCAML
let v = N.of_array [|2.; -0.5|] [|1; 2|]
let traj = ref (N.copy v)
let a = ref v
let eta = 0.0001
let n = 200;;

As preparation, we use an initial starting point [2, -0.5]. The step size eta is set to 0.0001, and n=200 stores the initial point and 199 updates. Then we can perform the iterative descent process. You can also run this process in a recursive manner.

OCAML
let _ =
  for i = 1 to n - 1 do
  let u = grad rosenbrock (Arr !a) |> unpack_arr in
  a := N.(sub !a (scalar_mul eta u));
  traj := N.concatenate [|!traj; (N.copy !a)|]
  done;;

We apply the grad method to the Rosenbrock function iteratively, and the updated data a is stored in the traj array. Finally, let’s visualise the trajectory of the optimisation process.

OCAML
let plot () =
  let a, b = Dense.Matrix.D.meshgrid (-2.) 2. (-1.) 3. 50 50 in
  let c = N.(scalar_mul 100.
    (pow_scalar (sub b (pow_scalar a 2.)) 2.) +
    (pow_scalar (scalar_sub 1. a) 2.)) in

  let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_gradients.png" in
  Plot.subplot h 0 0;
  Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ NoMagColor ] a b c);

  Plot.subplot h 0 1;
  Plot.contour ~h a b c;
  let vx = N.get_slice [[]; [0]] !traj in
  let vy = N.get_slice [[]; [1]] !traj in
  Plot.plot ~h vx vy;
  Plot.output h;;
plot ();;

We first create a mesh grid based on the Rosenbrock function to visualise the 3D image, then on the 2D contour image of the same function we plot how the result of the optimisation is updated, from the initial starting point towards a local minimum point. The visualisation results are shown in Fig. 9.4. On the right figure the black line shows the moving trajectory downwards along the slope towards the minimum; this finite run does not establish convergence.

Optimisation is the foundation of machine learning and neural network training. In the Owl_optimise.D module, we provide a minimise_fun function to perform this task. This function is exposed by the optimisation module and can minimise a scalar function of an AD array using the configured update method. This function is based on the Algorithmic Differentiation module. It minimises a function in the form of f: x → y with regard to x, an AD ndarray, and y is an AD scalar value. This function is implemented following the iterative descent approach. Let’s use the previous Rosenbrock function example to demonstrate how it works.

OCAML
let p = Owl_optimise.D.Params.default ()
let _ = p.epochs <- 10.
let _ = p.gradient <- Owl_optimise.D.Gradient.GD;;
p.learning_rate <- Owl_optimise.D.Learning_Rate.Const 0.001;;

First, we set the optimisation parameters. The Owl_optimise.D.Params sub-module contains several categories of parameters, including the gradient method, learning rate, loss functions, regularisation method, momentum method, epochs and batching. We will introduce these different parts in Chapter 10. For now it suffices simply to set the iteration limit epochs to something like 10 or 20 iterations. We set gradient descent and an explicit learning rate of 0.001, then execute the code from the same initial values:

OCAML
let init_value = N.of_array [|2.;-0.5|] [|1;2|] |> pack_arr
let optimisation_state, optimised = Owl_optimise.D.minimise_fun p rosenbrock init_value;;

This function outputs detailed logs to track the intermediate results. The entries below come from the actual container run; only timestamps, terminal colour and status-arrow decorations are omitted. Each line reports the loss before its corresponding update: the initial loss is 2026, and the tenth logged value is about 2.6 after nine updates. The returned point includes the tenth update; neither the log nor this short run establishes convergence.

OCAML SESSION
T: 00s | E: 1.0/10 | B: 1/10 | L: 2026.000000
T: 00s | E: 2.0/10 | B: 2/10 | L: 476.101033
T: 00s | E: 3.0/10 | B: 3/10 | L: 63.836145
T: 00s | E: 4.0/10 | B: 4/10 | L: 37.776798
T: 00s | E: 5.0/10 | B: 5/10 | L: 21.396863
T: 00s | E: 6.0/10 | B: 6/10 | L: 11.742345
T: 00s | E: 7.0/10 | B: 7/10 | L: 6.567733
T: 00s | E: 8.0/10 | B: 8/10 | L: 4.085909
T: 00s | E: 9.0/10 | B: 9/10 | L: 3.016714
T: 00s | E: 10.0/10 | B: 10/10 | L: 2.594318

9.4.3 Conjugate Gradient Method

Unfortunately, a problem with Gradient Descent is that it may perform badly on certain types of functions. For example, if a function is steep and narrow then gradient descent will take very many small steps to reach the minimum, bouncing back and forth, even if the function is in quadratic form.

This behaviour motivates the Conjugate Gradient (CG) method, first proposed by Hestenes and Stiefel [13]. The CG method is one of the most popular iterative methods to solve large – and particularly sparse – linear systems in the form of A𝐱 = b where system matrix A should be symmetric and positive-definite. The CG method is similar to gradient descent, but the new direction at each step does not completely follow the new gradient but combines the negative gradient with the previous search direction. For a positive-definite quadratic in exact arithmetic, the directions are A-conjugate: diTAdj = 0 for i≠j.

For example, Fig. 9.5 compares the descent efficiency of the conjugate gradient against gradient descent. Both methods start from the same position and move in the same direction. At the next point, gradient descent follows the new negative gradient, making a sharp turn across the narrow valley. But the conjugate method thinks, “hmm, this seems like a steep turn of direction, and I would prefer retaining some of the previous direction”. As a result, the conjugate method follows a direction in between (the red dotted line), and it turns out that the new direction avoids lots of unnecessary bounces and finds the minimum with fewer steps in this illustration. The coefficient is chosen by a conjugacy formula, not by an arbitrary momentum setting.

For the quadratic objective f(x) = 1 2xT𝐴𝑥 − bTx with symmetric positive-definite A, define the residual rn = b − Axn = −∇ ⁡f(xn) and initialise d0 = r0. Until the residual meets the stopping criterion, linear CG updates

αn = rnTrn dnTAdn, xn+1 = xn + αndn, rn+1 = rn − αnAdn, βn = rn+1Trn+1 rnTrn , dn+1 = rn+1 + βndn. (9.6)

Here xn is the current solution estimate, rn is the residual, and dn is the search direction. These are different quantities. For nonlinear objectives, related CG methods use gradient-based recurrences and a step-size strategy. Owl’s Owl_optimise.D.Gradient.CG selects a Hestenes–Stiefel-type nonlinear direction update; it does not by itself implement the exact quadratic line search above.

9.4.4 Newton and Quasi-Newton Methods

Newton’s method in optimisation applies the root-finding idea to the gradient, seeking a stationary point [14]. It follows the basic iteration structure, but its direction is a descent direction only under suitable conditions. The Newton method starts from an initial point and then repeats the process:

  1. solve for the Newton direction: ∇ ⁡2f(xn)d = −∇ ⁡f(xn);
  2. choose a step size α;
  3. update the location: xn+1 = xn + 𝛼𝑑.

We denote ∇ ⁡2f(xn) as the second-order derivatives of function f. For a scalar-valued function, its 2nd order derivatives can be represented by its Hessian matrix, which is introduced in Chap. 8. With the Hessian matrix 𝐇, the update process of Newton’s method can be expressed as:

xn+1 = xn − α𝐇𝐧−1∇ ⁡f(x n).

For a nonsingular Hessian this gives the Newton direction; a positive-definite Hessian ensures descent when the gradient is nonzero. In practice one normally solves a linear system rather than forming the inverse. The following small teaching example uses an explicit inverse and row-vector gradients, so the inverse appears on the right:

OCAML
open Algodiff.D;;
let newton ?(eta=F 0.01) ?(eps=1e-6) ?(max_iter=10000) f x =
  let rec loop remaining x =
    let g, h = gradhessian f x in
    let norm = Maths.l2norm' g |> unpack_flt in
    if not (Float.is_finite norm) then failwith "non-finite Newton gradient";
    if norm < eps then x
    else if remaining = 0 then failwith "Newton iteration limit"
    else
      loop (remaining - 1) Maths.(x - eta * g *@ (inv h))
  in loop max_iter x;;
let stationary_point =
  let f x = Maths.(cos x |> sum') in
  newton f (Mat.uniform 1 2);;
Mat.print stationary_point;;

A small gradient indicates approximate stationarity, which need not be a minimum. The cosine-sum example approaches (0,0), a local maximum, from the sampled initial values in [0,1). The implementation also has an iteration limit and rejects non-finite gradients.

With sufficiently smooth derivatives, a nonsingular Hessian at the solution and a sufficiently close starting point, the full Newton step (α = 1) has local quadratic convergence. The fixed damping α = 0.01 used above does not generally retain that rate. A major cost of a dense implementation is storing an n × n Hessian and solving the associated system. Sparse and matrix-free variants can reduce that cost, but forming and inverting a dense Hessian is impractical for millions of variables.

To avoid computing second derivatives explicitly, quasi-Newton methods build approximations to the Hessian or its inverse using changes in iterates and gradients. Under suitable assumptions, full BFGS can converge superlinearly, but there is no general rule that n quasi-Newton steps equal one Newton step. An important method in this category is BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno), named after its four developers [5]. Using a Hessian approximation Bi, its search direction di satisfies

Bidi = −∇ ⁡f(xi).

Here Bi is an n × n matrix, updated at each step. Full BFGS still requires quadratic storage. The limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) method [15] addresses this by retaining only a small number of recent iterate and gradient differences, from which it computes the inverse-Hessian action without storing a dense approximation.

9.5 Global Optimisation and Constrained Optimisation

So far we have focused on unconstrained optimisation, where we are trying to find local optima. In the rest of this chapter we will give a very brief introduction to global optimisation and constrained optimisation.

The basic idea of global optimisation is to provide search methods and heuristics to traverse the search space effectively. One method is to start from several initial points and find the local optima, then choose the smallest/largest value from them. Another heuristic is to try stepping away from a local optimal value by taking a finite amplitude step away from it, performing the optimisation method, and verifying if it leads to a better solution. These finite searches do not in general certify a global optimum.

An example of a global optimisation algorithm is the Simulated Annealing Method [16], inspired by the thermodynamics of metals cooling and annealing after being at a high temperature. Slow cooling can favour low-energy configurations, suggesting a way to search for low objective values. Simulated annealing has been applied to the NP-hard travelling salesman problem to seek short tours, without guaranteeing the shortest tour in a finite run.

A suitable system to apply Simulated Annealing has several elements, starting with a finite set S, and a cost function f that is defined on the set. There is also a non-increasing function T that projects the set of positive integers to real positive values. T(t) is called the temperature at time t. Suppose at time t, the current state is i in S. With a symmetric neighbour proposal, it randomly selects a neighbour j. For minimisation, if f(j) ≤ f(i) then j is accepted as the next state. Otherwise, j is chosen as the next state with a probability of e−f(j)−f(i) T(t) , otherwise the state remains i. Starting from an initial state x0, this process is repeated for a chosen number of steps while retaining the best state found. The cooling schedule and available run time affect the result.

Constrained Optimisation is another large optimisation topic. Unlike the optimisation problems we have seen so far, in a real-world problem it is hardly the case that you can freely explore the solution space with zero restriction, local or global. More often than not there will be constraints on the variables. The linear, convex and quadratic programmes introduced in Sec. 9.1 can all include constraints. If the objective and constraints are linear and the variables are required to be integers, the problem is called Integer Linear Programming (ILP); with both integer and continuous variables it is mixed-integer linear programming.

With the help of algorithms such as the simplex algorithm and interior point methods, linear programming problems can often be efficiently solved with existing methods and off-the-shelf tools. The tools such as LINDO [17] provide functionality to solve various sorts of optimisation problems. CVXOPT is a Python-based software package for convex optimization [18]. General scientific computing libraries and environments such as SciPy and MATLAB also provide optimisation tools.

Compared to linear optimisation, general nonlinear optimisation can be more challenging, particularly when the problem is non-convex. For smooth constrained problems, Lagrange multipliers and the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions [19, 20] characterise candidate optima under appropriate constraint qualifications. Continuity alone is not enough for the usual differentiable KKT conditions, and for non-convex problems these conditions are not generally sufficient for a global optimum. Nonsmooth or discrete problems also have specialised methods; simulated annealing is one option, not the only one.

Finding a global solution that maximises or minimises a non-linear objective function is often time-consuming, even for only a small set of variables. Therefore, global optimisation of a non-linear problem is normally only used when it is absolutely necessary. For example, suppose a system pressure test is modelled as an optimisation problem. Given a small number of variables in the system, a global extreme value has to be found to test if the system is robust enough. A local maximum or minimum can be useful as a candidate, but it cannot by itself certify such a worst-case bound. In many engineering applications, a local solution is useful when it meets the required accuracy and feasibility checks. Whether it is adequate depends on the task. Local methods often cost less than a global search, but their results can depend on algorithm parameters and the initial guess; a stopping test alone does not establish global optimality.

9.6 Summary

In this chapter we have given an overview of the mathematical optimisation field. Optimisation problems can be viewed in two dimensions: local or global, unconstrained or constrained. We primarily focused on the local unconstrained problem. In the beginning, we introduced techniques to find roots of functions, since the basic idea of root finding is similar to that of optimisation. Next, the local unconstrained problem was explained in two parts: univariate and multivariate optimisation, depending on the number of optimisation variables. An optimisation problem can be solved with or without calculating derivatives. We thus introduced methods in both aspects in these parts. Such methods include golden section search, Nelder-Mead, Newton’s method and gradient descent. Of all these methods, gradient descent is especially important and we will encounter it again in the regression and neural network chapters. Finally, we gave a brief introduction to the topic of global and constrained optimisation problems.
